title: Super-Multiplicativity of the Noncommutative Minimum and Applications to Quantum Privacy and Hypothesis Testing
authors: Theshani Nuradha, Sujeet Bhalerao, Christoph Hirche, Mark M. Wilde, Mingze Xu
problem: The hockey-stick divergence \(E_\gamma(\rho\|\sigma)=\mathrm{Tr}(\rho-\gamma\sigma)_+\) governs quantum differential privacy and the error of binary state discrimination with unequal priors. Unlike relative entropy it is not additive on product states, because the best test of \(\rho_1\otimes\rho_2\) against \(\sigma_1\otimes\sigma_2\) may be an entangled measurement. The known composition bound carries factors of \(\gamma\) that grow with each system, so it was unclear whether quantum privacy composes as cleanly as classical privacy when adversaries measure collectively.
result: The noncommutative minimum \(m(A,B)=\tfrac12(\mathrm{Tr}A+\mathrm{Tr}B-\|A-B\|_1)\) is super-multiplicative: \(m(A\otimes C,B\otimes D)\ge m(A,B)\,m(C,D)\) for all positive semidefinite operators. Consequently \(E_{\gamma_1\cdots\gamma_n}\) of a product is at most \(1-\prod_i(1-E_{\gamma_i})\), which is tight, and the parallel composition of \((\varepsilon_i,\delta_i)\)-private channels is \((\sum_i\varepsilon_i,\,1-\prod_i(1-\delta_i))\)-private even against collective measurements. The same tool gives the exact prefactor of the quantum Chernoff bound for noncommuting states under a nonlattice condition.
significance: Classical differential privacy composes by adding the \(\varepsilon\)'s and the \(\delta\)'s; the theorem shows this survives entangled attacks on product inputs, answering a question raised in earlier work on quantum privacy. The super-multiplicative inequality is a short structural fact that also yields sub-additivity of the Datta–Leditzky information-spectrum divergences and determines the sample complexity of symmetric state discrimination to within one copy.
limitations: Privacy composition is proved for product neighbouring inputs; correlated inputs across mechanisms are not covered. The inequality needs the parameters \(\gamma_i\) to multiply; with \(\gamma\) held fixed, sub-additivity fails. The refined Chernoff asymptotics assume an interior optimizer and a nonlattice condition that holds for generic noisy states but must be checked case by case, and that part of the paper was not read in detail here. The authors acknowledge the use of Claude Opus 5.5 and ChatGPT 6.1 Sol and 6.0 Astra in proof formulation, manuscript development, literature checks, figures and numerical tests.
summary_basis: Description based on the full arXiv HTML of v1, read 2026-11-25: Sec. 1 (contributions), Sec. 3 up to Proposition 3.10 including Lemmas 3.2–3.5, Theorem 3.6, Corollaries 3.8–3.9 and the proof sketch of Lemma 3.5, and the acknowledgements. Section 4 was read through the summary in Sec. 1 only, and the appendix proofs of Lemmas 3.4 and 3.5 were not read. Editorial checks: over 3000 random pairs of positive operators (dimensions 2 and 3, random ranks and traces, generally noncommuting) the smallest value of m(A⊗C, B⊗D) − m(A,B)m(C,D) was +8 × 10^-6; the three-system hockey-stick bound had no violation in 500 random qubit trials; a random search found qubit states with E_γ(ρ1⊗ρ2‖σ1⊗σ2) exceeding E_γ(ρ1‖σ1) + E_γ(ρ2‖σ2) by 0.26 at fixed γ, confirming that the parameters must multiply.

methods_basis: Based on the linked paper version. Derivations marked as editorial, and suggested uses in other problems, are editorial guidance rather than results of the paper.
description: Two weighted hypotheses \(A\) and \(B\) are distinguished by a test \(T\), and the smallest weighted error is \(\min_{0\le T\le I}\{\mathrm{Tr}AT+\mathrm{Tr}B(I-T)\}\), which equals the noncommutative minimum \(m(A,B)\). When \(A\) and \(B\) commute it is the sum of the smaller eigenvalues, \(\sum_x\min\{a_x,b_x\}\). For a state \(\rho\) and \(\gamma\ge1\), \(m(\rho,\gamma\sigma)=1-E_\gamma(\rho\|\sigma)\), and \(m(p\rho,(1-p)\sigma)\) is the optimal error of discrimination with priors \(p\) and \(1-p\).

The central theorem says weighted errors multiply at worst: discriminating products is never more than the product of the separate errors easier, even with an entangled measurement across both systems. For commuting operators this is the elementary \(\min\{ac,bd\}\ge\min\{a,b\}\min\{c,d\}\). The difficulty is that the optimal product test need not factorize, and the proof avoids it by splitting each pair into rank-one pairs whose errors add up exactly.

Translated into divergences, the theorem gives \(E_{\Gamma}(\otimes_i\rho_i\|\otimes_i\sigma_i)\le1-\prod_i(1-E_{\gamma_i})\le\sum_iE_{\gamma_i}\) with \(\Gamma=\prod_i\gamma_i\). Read as probabilities, the product leaks at level \(\Gamma\) no more often than at least one of independent events with probabilities \(E_{\gamma_i}\) occurs. The bound is attained for every value of the divergences, also by noncommuting states, and it is strict for faithful states when two or more divergences are positive.

Three applications follow. Parallel composition of quantum differentially private channels keeps the classical parameters against collective measurements. A normalized hypothesis-testing relative entropy becomes super-multiplicative, giving a converse valid for every number of copies. And for symmetric discrimination of \(n\) copies the paper derives the prefactor \(A_q\) in \(P_e\approx A_q e^{-n\xi}/\sqrt n\), removing a factor-of-two uncertainty left by Cheng and Liu, together with higher-order corrections.

methods.explanation: A general pair \((A,B)\) is split into rank-one pairs \((A_i,B_i)\) whose individual minima add up to \(m(A,B)\) exactly. Super-additivity of \(m\) under sums then reduces the product inequality to rank-one operators, where it is a scalar computation.
math: Super-additivity is the triangle inequality: \[m\Bigl(\sum_iA_i,\sum_iB_i\Bigr)=\tfrac12\Bigl(\sum_i\mathrm{Tr}A_i+\sum_i\mathrm{Tr}B_i-\Bigl\|\sum_i(A_i-B_i)\Bigr\|_1\Bigr)\ge\sum_im(A_i,B_i).\] Equality holds when the differences \(A_i-B_i\) do not cancel in trace norm, that is when the positive part of every \(A_i-B_i\) lies in the positive spectral subspace of \(A-B\) and the negative part in the negative one. Then the projector onto the positive part of \(B-A\) is an optimal test for every pair simultaneously.

The paper first removes a common part \(C_0\le A,B\), after which the ranges of \(A-C_0\) and \(B-C_0\) meet only at zero, and then builds rank-one pairs with this sign alignment. Given such decompositions of \((A,B)\) and \((C,D)\), \[m(A\otimes C,B\otimes D)\ge\sum_{i,j}m(A_i\otimes C_j,B_i\otimes D_j)\ge\sum_{i,j}m(A_i,B_i)\,m(C_j,D_j)=m(A,B)\,m(C,D),\] using super-additivity, the rank-one case and exactness of the decompositions.

Editorial check: random noncommuting positive operators of dimensions 2 and 3 never violated the inequality in 3000 trials, and the smallest gap found was positive. The rank-one case, proved in an appendix, is where noncommutativity is handled explicitly; it is strict when both pairs are nonzero, non-proportional and have positive minimum.
methods.transfer: Decomposing an operator pair into pieces that share one optimal test, so that a nonlinear quantity becomes additive across the pieces, is a general route from rank-one inequalities to full ones. It applies to other trace-norm functionals of pairs of operators.

methods.technique: From weighted errors to privacy composition
methods.explanation: Privacy at level \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) is a bound on a hockey-stick divergence with \(\gamma=e^\varepsilon\). Writing that divergence as one minus a noncommutative minimum turns super-multiplicativity of the minimum into a composition rule in which the \(\gamma\)'s multiply and the \(\delta\)'s combine like independent failure probabilities.
math: A channel \(\mathcal A\) is \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-private if \(E_{e^\varepsilon}(\mathcal A(\rho)\|\mathcal A(\sigma))\le\delta\) for all neighbouring inputs. For product neighbours, apply the theorem with \(A=\rho_1'\), \(B=e^{\varepsilon_1}\sigma_1'\), \(C=\rho_2'\), \(D=e^{\varepsilon_2}\sigma_2'\), where primes denote channel outputs: \[1-E_{e^{\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2}}(\rho_1'\otimes\rho_2'\|\sigma_1'\otimes\sigma_2')\ge(1-\delta_1)(1-\delta_2).\] So the parallel composition is \((\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2,\,1-(1-\delta_1)(1-\delta_2))\)-private, and \(1-(1-\delta_1)(1-\delta_2)\le\delta_1+\delta_2\).

The earlier general bound, \(E_{\gamma_1\gamma_2}\le E_{\gamma_1}+\gamma_1E_{\gamma_2}\), comes from a triangle inequality and puts a factor \(\gamma_1=e^{\varepsilon_1}\) in front of the second divergence, which is large in the low-privacy regime. The new bound has no such factor and is symmetric in the two systems.

The parameters must multiply. Editorial check: at a fixed \(\gamma\), a random search over qubit states found \(E_\gamma(\rho_1\otimes\rho_2\|\sigma_1\otimes\sigma_2)\) exceeding \(E_\gamma(\rho_1\|\sigma_1)+E_\gamma(\rho_2\|\sigma_2)\) by 0.26, in line with the paper's Example 3.17.
methods.transfer: Expressing a one-shot divergence as the optimal weighted error of a test, and composing errors rather than divergences, is a route to composition theorems for other privacy and security notions defined by hockey-stick or smoothed divergences.
